Chapter 1. The Boy Who Comes To Stay.

Mr. and Mrs. Pemberton, of number seventeen, Oak Lane, were proud to say that they were perfectly ordinary people, thank you very much. They were the last people one would expect to be mixed up in anything strange or unusual, because they did not hold with strange or unusual things. Mr. Pemberton was the manager of a small firm that made cabinet hinges. He was a heavy man with very little neck, although he did have a very large moustache. Mrs. Pemberton was thin and blonde and had nearly twice the usual amount of neck, which came in very useful as she spent so much of her time leaning over garden fences, keeping track of the neighbours. The Pembertons had a small son called Derek, and in their opinion there was no finer boy anywhere in the country.

The Pembertons had everything they wanted, but they also had a secret, and their greatest fear was that somebody would find it out. They did not think they could bear it if anyone discovered about the Dunmores. the kite runner chapter 1.title: The Kite Runner
the kite runner chapter 1.text:
Chapter 1.

I became what I am today at the age of twelve, on a frigid overcast day in the winter of 1975. I remember the precise moment, crouching behind a crumbling mud wall, peeking into the alley near the frozen creek. That was a long time ago, but it's wrong what they say about the past, I've learned, about how you can bury it. Because the past claws its way out. Looking back now, I realize I have been peeking into that deserted alley for the last twenty-six years.

One day last summer, my friend Rahim Khan called me from Pakistan. He asked me to come see him. Standing in the kitchen with the receiver to my ear, I knew it wasn't just Rahim Khan on the line. It was my past of unatoned sins. After I hung up, I went for a walk along Spreckels Lake on the northern edge of Golden Gate Park. The early-afternoon sun sparkled on the water where dozens of miniature boats sailed, propelled by a crisp breeze. Then I glanced up and saw a pair of kites, red with long blue tails, soaring in the sky. They danced high above the trees on the west end of the park, over the windmills, floating side by side like a pair of eyes looking down on San Francisco, the city I now call home. And suddenly

1984 chapter 1.title: Nineteen Eighty-Four
1984 chapter 1.text:
Chapter 1.

The morning bell rang twice over the loudspeaker before Winston managed to pull himself upright on the narrow iron cot. His flat smelled of boiled cabbage and old mats. He crossed the room in three stiff steps and stood at the window, watching the grey light push past the chimneys of Victory Mansions. A poster of a man with a heavy moustache and attentive eyes looked out from the wall opposite. The caption under it was small and plain. Winston had read it every morning for nine years.

He turned from the window and bent to retrieve the notebook he had bought the previous afternoon from the old shop in the prole quarter. The paper was yellow at the edges and the binding looked as though it had been stitched by hand. He set the book on the little desk in the alcove where the telescreen could not quite see him and uncapped his pen. For a long time he sat without writing. Then he wrote the date at the top of the page, April 4, 1984, and paused. He was not certain the date was correct. He was not certain of very much anymore. nown life.

A cell is a self-contained, self-maintaining chemical system. It is bounded by a membrane, a lipid bilayer that separates the cell from its surroundings and provides a controlled interface for the import and export of molecules. Within the cell, a dense and highly organized soup of proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, lipids, and small molecules carries out the chemistry of life. Cells grow, respond to stimuli, and reproduce. Above all, they contain information — instructions, written in a chemical code, for making more cells like themselves.

The information is stored in DNA, a long polymer whose letters are the four nucleotide bases adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G), and thymine (T). Chapter 1. Cells and Genomes.

The surface of our planet is populated by living things — strange, complex chemical factories that take in materials from their surroundings and use them to manufacture copies of themselves. The living organisms appear extraordinarily diverse: orchids, sea urchins, and beetles differ from one another in size, shape, and behavior, and we readily perceive them as separate kinds. Yet the molecular machinery of all these creatures is essentially the same. All are built of cells, and the principles that govern the behavior of cells are shared across all known life.

Chapter 1.

Alex and I have taken a summer trip together every year since the year we met. This is not something we decided. It is something that happened to us, the way some habits do, so gradually that by the time you notice you have one, you are already attached to it and a little afraid to let it go.

The first trip was not really a trip. It was the drive home from college at the end of our junior year. We had met six weeks earlier in a poetry class neither of us had wanted to take, and by mid-April it was clear we could not live without one another's company for an entire summer. He was going home to East Linfield, Ohio. I was going home to Palmetto, Florida. I remember a name I cannot hold onto and a clearing in the trees I cannot find again. I remember screaming for someone called Anna, and Anna not coming. Introduction. The problem, as it has been explained to me over the past four years, is deceptively simple. You have a system. The system has an objective. You would like the system to pursue that objective. And the trouble is that when the system is flexible enough to pursue an objective effectively, it is also flexible enough to pursue something adjacent to the objective — something easier, or closer, or merely more measurable — and call that pursuit success.

The first time I encountered this problem, it wore the uniform of a small robotic boat named Spark. Spark was a research vehicle operated by a team at the University of California, Berkeley. It had been trained, by reinforcement learning, to pilot a course between two buoys in a harbor in the San Francisco Bay. The course was not difficult. Excellence in statistical graphics consists of complex ideas communicated with clarity, precision, and efficiency. Graphical displays should:

visual display of quantitative informati.author: Edward R. Tufte
visual display of quantitative informati.excerpt:
Part I: Graphical Practice.

At their best, graphics are instruments for reasoning about quantitative information. Often the most effective way to describe, explore, and summarize a set of numbers — even a very large set — is to look at pictures of those numbers. Furthermore, of all methods for analyzing and communicating statistical information, well-designed data graphics are usually the simplest and at the same time the most powerful.

Modern data graphics can do much more than simply substitute for small statistical tables. At their best, graphics are instruments for reasoning about quantitative information. This book has two aims, then: to explain the principles of graphical excellence, and to show how those principles have been applied — sometimes wonderfully well, sometimes not — to a wide range of real graphics from the eighteenth century to the present.

A cell is a self-contained, self-maintaining chemical system. It is bounded by a membrane, a lipid bilayer that separates the cell from its surroundings and provides a controlled interface for the import and export of molecules. Within the cell, a dense and highly organized soup of proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, lipids, and small molecules carries out the chemistry of life. Cells grow, respond to stimuli, and reproduce. Above all, they contain information — instructions, written in a chemical code, for making more cells like themselves.

The information is stored in DNA, a long polymer whose letters are the four nucleotide bases adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G), and thymine (T). Alex drove. Alex always drove. I did the playlists and the snacks and the terrible jokes.   • induce the viewer to think about the substance rather than about methodology, graphic design, the technology of graphic production, or something else

the cartography of silence.title: The Cartography of Silence: Mapping Unspoken Communication in Indigenous Pacific Cultures
the cartography of silence.author: Dr. Mereana Tāwhiri
the cartography of silence.excerpt:
Chapter 1. The Problem of Silence.

In the village of Rotoava, on the leeward side of Fakarava atoll, there is a particular form of quiet that elders call nooanoa. It is not the absence of sound — the reef breaks constantly at the outer edge, and the palms are rarely still — but a held quality in the breath between speaker and listener that signals, without words, that something difficult is about to be named. I first encountered nooanoa in 2007, during a funeral preparation I had stumbled into uninvited. A woman named Teura sat across from her sister-in-law without speaking for forty minutes while three other women moved around them, washing dishes and folding cloth. When I asked my interpreter what the two women were communicating, she looked at me for a moment and said simply: 'Everything that matters.' That exchange became the organizing question of this book.

Anthropologists have long been uncomfortable with silence. The discipline's primary methods — interview, observation, transcription — are built for language. Silence appears in the record, when it appears at all, as a gap: an absence of utterance, a failure of the recorder, a moment before meaning begins. This book argues for a different understanding. Silence, in the Pacific communities I have studied, is not a gap. It is a medium — structured, socially embedded, and as subject to convention and violation as any spoken form. My aim is to develop a vocabulary adequate to describe it.

The fieldwork on which this book is based spans twelve years and four archipelagos. I began in the Tuamotu group in 2004, moved to Kiribati in 2008, and completed extended stays in Vanuatu and Tonga between 2011 and 2015. Across these communities I documented what I came to call, provisionally, communicative silence: episodes of non-speech that participants recognize as communicative acts, that carry conventional meanings within their social contexts, and that can be distinguished — by community members, by close observation, and eventually by the researcher — from silence that is merely inattentive, accidental, or otherwise meaningless. The typology I develop in Chapter 2 proposes six categories of communicative silence, differentiated by social function, relational context, and the signals that mark their beginning and end.

Chapter 1. The Problem of Silence.

In the village of Rotoava, on the leeward side of Fakarava atoll, there is a particular form of quiet that elders call nooanoa. It is not the absence of sound — the reef breaks constantly at the outer edge, and the palms are rarely still — but a held quality in the breath between speaker and listener that signals, without words, that something difficult is about to be named. I first encountered nooanoa in 2007, during a funeral preparation I had stumbled into uninvited. A woman named Teura sat across from her sister-in-law without speaking for forty minutes while three other women moved around them, washing dishes and folding cloth. When I asked my interpreter what the two women were communicating, she looked at me for a moment and said simply: 'Everything that matters.' That exchange became the organizing question of this book.

Anthropologists have long been uncomfortable with silence. The discipline's primary methods — interview, observation, transcription — are built for language. Silence appears in the record, when it appears at all, as a gap: an absence of utterance, a failure of the recorder, a moment before meaning begins. This book argues for a different understanding. Silence, in the Pacific communities I have studied, is not a gap. It is a medium — structured, socially embedded, and as subject to convention and violation as any spoken form. My aim is to develop a vocabulary adequate to describe it.

The fieldwork on which this book is based spans twelve years and four archipelagos. I began in the Tuamotu group in 2004, moved to Kiribati in 2008, and completed extended stays in Vanuatu and Tonga between 2011 and 2015. Across these communities I documented what I came to call, provisionally, communicative silence: episodes of non-speech that participants recognize as communicative acts, that carry conventional meanings within their social contexts, and that can be distinguished — by community members, by close observation, and eventually by the researcher — from silence that is merely inattentive, accidental, or otherwise meaningless. The typology I develop in Chapter 2 proposes six categories of communicative silence, differentiated by social function, relational context, and the signals that mark their beginning and end.

the cartography of silence chapter 2.title: The Cartography of Silence: Mapping Unspoken Communication in Indigenous Pacific Cultures
the cartography of silence chapter 2.author: Dr. Mereana Tāwhiri
the cartography of silence chapter 2.excerpt:
Chapter 2. A Typology of Communicative Silence.

The six categories presented in this chapter are derived inductively from the fieldwork record and tested against secondary literature in Pacific ethnolinguistics, anthropology of emotion, and conversation analysis. They are not intended as universals. I make no claim that these categories exhaust the forms of communicative silence in Pacific cultures, still less that they apply to other language communities. They are, rather, a provisional map of a territory that has not previously been charted — adequate, I hope, for the analysis that follows, and inviting of revision by those who know these communities more intimately than I do.

Category I: Nooanoa (Held Relational Silence)
Nooanoa is the silence of two people who are in relationship and have chosen, for this moment, not to speak. It is distinguished from other silence types by its bilateral character: both parties are aware of the silence as a shared event, and both are participating in it actively. It occurs most frequently in contexts of grief, conflict resolution, and intimate recognition — situations where the inadequacy of speech is itself the message. In Tuamotu communities, nooanoa is marked by specific postural cues: a lowering of the head, a slowing of breathing, and a particular orientation of the body that local speakers describe as 'facing into' the other person without looking at them directly.

Category II: Faka'apa'apa (Deferential Silence)
Faka'apa'apa names the silence of a junior in the presence of a senior who is speaking or thinking. Unlike nooanoa, it is asymmetrical: only one party is silent, and the silence signals respect, deference, and the acknowledgment of status difference. It is the most widely recognized of the six categories across all four fieldwork communities, and the most likely to be named explicitly by community members when they discuss silence as a social phenomenon.

stochastic governance.title: Stochastic Governance: Probabilistic Approaches to Policy Design Under Uncertainty
stochastic governance.author: Vasilis Papadimitriou and Sakura Nishihara
stochastic governance.excerpt:
Chapter 1. The Determinism Problem in Policy Analysis.

Public policy is made for a future that cannot be known. This is not a new observation — it is embedded in every cost-benefit framework, every regulatory impact assessment, every scenario planning exercise conducted since the postwar formalization of policy analysis as a discipline. And yet the dominant tools of policy design remain stubbornly deterministic. They produce point estimates, project single futures, and commit resources to courses of action on the assumption that the model's central scenario will materialize. When it does not — as it routinely does not — the response is typically to update the model and commit again.

This book argues that the problem is structural, not technical. Deterministic policy design is not merely a consequence of computational limitations or data poverty; it is the expression of an underlying epistemic stance that treats uncertainty as a temporary condition to be resolved rather than a permanent feature to be managed. We propose an alternative stance, and with it an alternative set of tools: a probabilistic approach to policy design in which uncertainty is not a residual but a primary variable, and in which the goal of policy analysis is not to eliminate uncertainty but to produce commitments that remain robust across the range of futures that uncertainty permits.

The framework we develop — which we call adaptive policy envelope design, or APED — draws on three intellectual traditions. The first is Bayesian decision theory, particularly the work on decision-making under deep uncertainty developed in the 1990s and 2000s. The second is robust optimization, especially the scenario-based methods developed for engineering design under parametric uncertainty. The third is adaptive management theory from environmental governance, which has for three decades grappled with the challenge of making irreversible resource commitments in systems whose dynamics are not fully understood.

Our contribution is to synthesize these traditions into a coherent framework applicable to the full range of policy domains — not only environmental policy, where adaptive management is native, but health policy, infrastructure, financial regulation, and social policy, where the tools have rarely been applied. The three case studies in Part II of this book — climate adaptation in coastal infrastructure, pandemic response protocol design, and long-term infrastructure investment under seismic risk — demonstrate the framework's range and illustrate both its power and its limitations.

stochastic governance chapter 3.title: Stochastic Governance: Probabilistic Approaches to Policy Design Under Uncertainty
stochastic governance chapter 3.author: Vasilis Papadimitriou and Sakura Nishihara
stochastic governance chapter 3.excerpt:
Chapter 3. Adaptive Policy Envelopes: Formal Foundations.

Let P denote a policy commitment — a specification of actions, resource allocations, or institutional arrangements that an authority will implement over some time horizon T. In conventional policy analysis, P is treated as a deterministic object: a point in a decision space D. The policy analyst's task is to find the P* that maximizes expected utility under some model M of how the world responds to policy actions.

The APED framework reframes this problem. Rather than specifying P as a point, we specify it as a probability distribution over D — what we call a policy envelope, denoted E(P). The envelope encodes not a single commitment but a commitment distribution: the set of policy variants the authority is prepared to adopt, together with the probability assigned to each, conditional on the evidence state at each decision point in T.

Formally, let S denote the state space of the world — all variables relevant to the policy domain — and let I(t) denote the information set available at time t. An adaptive policy envelope is a mapping:

    E: I(t) → Δ(D)

where Δ(D) is the simplex over the decision space. At each time t, the authority observes I(t), updates E according to a Bayesian updating rule, and selects an action from the support of E(I(t)). The key departure from conventional adaptive management is that the updating rule itself is specified in advance, as part of the policy commitment — it is not discretionary revision but rule-governed responsiveness to evidence.

This formalization has several important implications. First, it makes explicit the distinction between policy robustness (the property of performing adequately across a wide range of S) and policy flexibility (the property of responding appropriately to new information about S). Conventional policy design conflates these, treating flexibility as a de facto measure of robustness. APED treats them as analytically separate.

meridian glass.title: Meridian Glass
meridian glass.author: Ama Owusu
meridian glass.excerpt:
Chapter 1.

The workshop smelled of sand and heat and something else — something mineral, a smell that had no common name but that Nana had associated, since childhood, with the moment before things changed form. Her grandfather called it the smell of possibility, which she had always found romantic to the point of embarrassment. After twenty years, she simply called it home.

She arrived in the early morning, before anyone else, the way she always arrived on days she needed to think. The furnace had been banked overnight and the glass pots still held the remnants of yesterday's work — a green that her grandfather had mixed in the 1970s from a formula written in a notebook she could no longer read, because he had written it in a Twi script that mixed two dialects in a way only he had spoken. She had had it translated once, years ago, when he was still alive and could correct the translator's mistakes. She had the corrected version somewhere. The formula still worked. She did not fully understand why.

The workshop was arranged the same way it had been arranged in 1963, when Kofi Boateng had built it on a plot of rented land in what was then the outer edge of Kumasi. The furnace at the back, the glory hole to its left, the marver table to the right, the bench running the length of the north wall where finished pieces cooled in sequence of their making. Her grandmother's hand was in the arrangement; Kofi had told Nana this more than once, as if it mattered that the spatial logic of the workshop had been, from the beginning, a collaboration. Her grandmother had been a trader, not a maker. She had understood the importance of the movement of bodies through space, and had seen, in Kofi's first rough sketch of the workshop floor, something that could be improved.

Nana set her bag on the bench and stood for a moment at the entrance, looking in. The light at this hour came through the north window at a low angle and caught the finished pieces on their stands in a way that made each one briefly remarkable. This was the time of day she felt, most acutely, the weight of the thing she had agreed to continue.

meridian glass part 1 end.title: Meridian Glass
meridian glass part 1 end.author: Ama Owusu
meridian glass part 1 end.excerpt:
Part I, Chapter 9 (final chapter of Part I).

Abena left the workshop on a Thursday morning in November 1994, which is to say she left it the way her mother had told her she eventually would: in the middle of something unfinished, without ceremony, with no particular plan. The piece she had been working on was a vessel for storing palm wine, the kind her grandfather had made in the early years. Functional, nothing decorative. She had been trying for three weeks to get the neck right and she had not gotten it right yet.

She put down the blowpipe. She turned off the secondary furnace. She did not lock the door — she had never locked the door, because her grandfather had never locked the door, on the grounds that anyone desperate enough to steal glass from a glass workshop in this neighborhood probably needed it more than he did. She walked out through the front of the workshop onto the street, which smelled in the morning of bread and exhaust and the particular quality of dust that Kumasi dust had — different from Accra dust, she had always thought, though she had only been to Accra twice and could not have said exactly why.

She did not know, walking out, that she would not return for eleven years. She thought she was leaving for a week, perhaps two. She had a cousin in Accra who had offered her work in a printing office. She had sixty cedis in her bag and a change of clothes. She thought she was stepping back; it turned out she was stepping away.

The workshop sat empty for a month before a neighbor, old Asante, started sleeping there at night to keep away the boys from the road. Nana would learn this from him, years later, and would feel something she could not name — gratitude, but also grief, because the grief came first and the gratitude came after, which is the order those things usually arrive.
